entry.title: Advice is autobiography.
entry.dek: Let 1.000 people try a pure 50/50 decision once and 500 will honestly tell you it works. Most advice is one life, and the useful question is what it cost.
body: “Every piece of advice is somebody’s past, told to you as your future.”

Have you ever asked yourself whose life a piece of advice is actually about? Today is Monday, the 16th of November, and since I turned eighteen I have been told to study something “safe”, to buy an apartment as soon as I can because “rent is throwing money away”, to stay away from the stock market because “it is a casino”, and, of course, to take risks while I am young. Every single one came from somebody who cares about me, and every single one was said with total confidence. So the question is: if all of them are sure, how can all of them be right? Let’s start from the beginning.

I met the answer, or at least the beginning of it, in the first chapter of “The Psychology of Money”, the one called “No One’s Crazy”. In my review I wrote about compound interest and Warren Buffett, but this chapter starts with a line I keep coming back to: “Your personal experiences with money make up maybe 0.00000001% of what’s happened in the world, but maybe 80% of how you think the world works.” Housel then talks about a study by two economists, Ulrike Malmendier and Stefan Nagel, published in 2011 with the title “Depression Babies”. What they found is that the stock market returns people lived through in their own lives shaped how much risk they were willing to take later, no matter what happened to the market before they were born. People do not give advice from the world, they give it from their world.

Firstly, let’s split the title in two, the way I like to do. “Advice” and “autobiography”. Advice sounds like it is about you - your future, your choices, what you should do next. Autobiography is about the person talking - their past, their choices, what happened to them. My point is that most of the time it is the second one dressed up as the first. When somebody says “rent is throwing money away”, they are usually not describing the housing market, they are describing their own life - the year they bought, the price they paid, the city they never wanted to leave. That does not make it wrong. It makes it one life, and one life is a very small study.

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic, because this is where it surprised me. This is an example I built, not a measurement. Imagine a decision that is a pure coin flip - it works for half of the people who try it, and fails for the other half, with no skill at all. Now take 1.000 people who each try it once.
1.000 × 0.5 = 500 people for whom it worked
1.000 × 0.5 = 500 people for whom it did not
Ask them for advice and you get 500 people telling you “do it, it worked for me” and 500 telling you “never do it”, all of them completely honest. Same decision, same odds, two opposite pieces of advice. An honest person with one result can still be giving you a coin flip.

And it does not get much better with more tries. Say every one of those 1.000 people made the same decision three times, still on pure chance. The probability of three good results in a row is 0.53 = 0.125, so:
1.000 × 0.125 = 125 people with a perfect record of three out of three
That is 125 people who will tell you, with real experience behind it, that they “always” got it right (yes, you read that right, with zero skill involved). And most big decisions in life are not made three times. You choose a university once, maybe a career once or twice, you buy an apartment once or twice. The advice that sounds the most experienced is often based on a sample of one or two.

This is why I think the best filter is a question, and I took it from the risk article I wrote on Friday the 13th, where the question was what you can afford to lose. When somebody gives me advice, I want to ask: “What did it cost you?” Not to be rude, but because the cost is the part that always gets cut. “I studied only the night before and I passed” sounds very different when you learn it was the second try. “Buy, don’t rent” sounds very different when you learn what the monthly payment did to the next twenty years. The result travels in the advice. The price stays with the person who paid it.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Autobiography is not nothing. The people older than me lived through things I have only read about, and when they tell me to keep some money aside “just in case”, that is not a coin flip, that is often something they saw happen to many people around them, not only to themselves. Experience is still evidence, it is just evidence from a small number of cases. And there is a trap on the other side too. If I decide that all advice is only autobiography, then the only life left to learn from is mine, and at eighteen that is the smallest sample of all. Ignoring everybody is not independence, it is just trusting a different autobiography - my own.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. Until the end of the year, every time somebody gives me a serious piece of advice, I will write it down with two questions next to it: “How many times did you try this?” and “What did it cost you?”. And I will apply the same filter to this blog, because every article here is advice from one eighteen-year-old with one life, and you should read it that way too.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that most advice says more about the person giving it than about the person getting it, and that the price is the most useful part and the one that is almost always missing. But I have to be honest about two things. My coin example is extreme on purpose - real decisions are not pure luck, and some people really did learn something true from a single result. And “what did it cost you?” is a question that is easy to ask and hard to hear, especially from somebody who gave up a lot to be able to give you that advice. What I take from it is smaller: listen to the story, but ask about the price before you copy the result.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Every piece of advice is somebody’s past, told to you as your future.”
